specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that word-embedding evaluation should emphasize transfer-usefulness by measuring data efficiency (learning curves over multiple training-set sizes summarized by AUC or similar), using simple supervised probe tasks (single-word classification, supervised/learnable similarity and analogy), and evaluating multiple model classes (constant/linear/nonlinear) to detect nonlinear encodings. Theoretical appendix (Observation 1) shows injective embeddings preserve Bayes risk, motivating focus on learnability under limited data and restricted hypothesis classes. Empirically, the authors run repeated-split experiments on ~15 datasets across four categories using several publicly available embeddings and model families. Principal empirical findings: supervised learnable versions of similarity and analogy can improve performance over constant baselines (reported ≈11% on a subset for analogy); embedding rankings change with dataset size and model class (mean rank change ≈0.6 across experiments); some embeddings encode information nonlinearly so nonlinear models can outperform linear ones; single-word properties are learned quickly (high accuracy at small sample sizes) while analogy tasks remain difficult. The proposal is coherent and presents an actionable evaluation protocol, but several operational choices and statistical/experimental controls are under-specified (vocabulary intersection/lowercasing, ANOVA ranking procedure, hyperparameter tuning fairness, leakage/overfitting controls for learnable probes). I tag claims as supported, partially supported, or overstated below, include alternative interpretations, and give concrete suggestions for strengthening evidentiary support and reproducibility.

evidence: Authors report mean absolute rank change ≈0.6 (std 0.2) and give examples of start/end ranks per embedding in Tables 1 and 3.
Figures show rank differences across tasks and that nonlinear models alter ordering for some embeddings.
uncertainty_flags: Magnitude (0.6) is reported without clear normalization/scale context of rank range and without statistical testing of rank-change significance across tasks.
Averaging across heterogeneous tasks may mask systematic behavior in particular task classes; some tasks show small rank change (Single-word) while others large (Analogy).

identified_claims.claim_text: Some embeddings encode information nonlinearly, so including nonlinear downstream models (in addition to linear ones) is necessary; cosine-based unsupervised evaluations can miss such nonlinear encodings.
evidence: Figure 1 and §3.6 document cases where non-linear models outperform linear ones; GloVe variants show different behavior early vs. late in learning.
Authors argue algebraic structure may be stored in subspaces requiring nonlinear extraction.
uncertainty_flags: Nonlinear model gains may come from higher capacity or overfitting rather than intrinsic nonlinear encoding; capacity-controlled comparisons (regularized kernels, shallow nets) not fully reported.
Preprocessing (normalization/intersection) could influence linear separability and therefore the observed nonlinear gains.

identified_claims.claim_text: Simple single-word properties (e.g., POS, sentiment, color associations) are quickly recoverable with high accuracy even with small amounts of data; learning curves show small gains from further training.
evidence: Table 3 shows high average accuracy and low rank-change for Single-word tasks; §3.7 notes single-word average accuracy ≈80% and little gain from fitting classifiers (~2%).
uncertainty_flags: Per-dataset class balance, number of labels, and variance of accuracy are not fully shown; some single-word properties might be easier due to dataset composition.
Generality to other single-word properties or languages not tested.

identified_claims.claim_text: There is no universally best embedding; embedding suitability depends on target application, dataset size, and model class, so evaluation should be targeted.
evidence: Observed task-dependent ordering and rank volatility; prior literature cited supports task dependence.
Empirical tables show different embeddings winning different tasks or regimes.
uncertainty_flags: Conclusion follows from tested set but remains conditional on embedding selection and task suite; extension to contextual embeddings or fine-tuned representations untested.

identified_claims.claim_text: Any injective embedding preserves all information about the task (Bayes risk is preserved), therefore differences between embeddings arise from how easily o' can be learned under limited data or constrained hypothesis class.
evidence: Appendix A provides formal proof: inverse mapping recovers original Bayes risk for injective E.
Discussion highlights practical relevance: complexity of inferring o' and convergence rates under finite samples.
uncertainty_flags: Injectivity assumption holds in discrete finite vocabularies, but preprocessing steps (vocab intersection, lowercasing) and embedding collisions can break it; empirical frequency of non-injectivity is not measured.
In continuous input spaces or dimensionality reduction cases (D' < D) injectivity is unlikely, limiting applicability of the theoretical guarantee.

strengths.title: Clear transfer-learning motivated reframing
strengths.description: The paper convincingly reframes embedding evaluation toward data efficiency and learnability under limited data, aligning evaluation objectives with practical transfer goals.
evidence: Formal objective in Eq. (1) and Appendix Observation 1 linking injectivity to Bayes risk preservation.
Motivation in §2 arguing sample complexity and extractability matter for transfer.

strengths.title: Actionable experimental protocol
strengths.description: Authors provide an implementable protocol (learning curves, model diversity, supervised probes) and compute per-embedding learning curves with repeated splits and AUC summaries.
evidence: §3 Experiments describes datasets, models, split strategy, and AUC/rank summaries; code/results promised.
Appendix B details a trainable analogy regressor (initialization as 3COSADD).

strengths.title: Demonstration that supervised intrinsic tasks add signal
strengths.description: Empirical results show learnable similarity and analogy probes can improve over constant baselines and uncover relations missed by cosine heuristics.
evidence: §3.4 reports ≈11% average improvement for regression NN on analogy subsets and SVR improvements on similarity.
Figures comparing constant vs supervised models on SimLex and WordRep subsets.

concerns.title: Ranking procedure and ANOVA assumptions under-specified
concerns.description: The greedy sequential ranking that groups embeddings using pairwise ANOVA at each curve point lacks detail on assumption checks (normality, homoscedasticity), multiple-comparison correction, and sensitivity analyses; this raises concern that reported ranks and their changes may be artifacts of the statistical procedure.
evidence: §3.3: "Ranks of embeddings at each point are calculated using a greedy sequential procedure... if their scores ... are not significantly different, as tested using pairwise ANOVA test."
SHARED_ANALYSIS and prior reviewers flagged potential ANOVA assumption violations and missing multiple-comparison detail.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report diagnostics for ANOVA assumptions (normality/homoscedasticity), apply nonparametric alternatives (Kruskal-Wallis, pairwise Wilcoxon with correction) or use permutation tests; show consistency of ranks under alternative statistical procedures and correct for multiple comparisons (e.g., Holm-Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg).

concerns.title: Hyperparameter tuning fairness and transparency
concerns.description: Hyperparameter search budgets, ranges, and whether the same tuning effort was applied across embeddings and models are not fully described; unequal tuning could bias measured data-efficiency or model-class sensitivity.
evidence: §3.1 mentions cross-validation for analogy NN and that nonlinear models include fallback to simpler models, but per-pair tuning budgets and search procedures are not detailed.
PRIOR_STAGE_DIGEST reviewers 1–4 flagged tuning fairness concerns.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Specify hyperparameter search spaces, budgets, random seeds, and per-embedding-model allocation; preferably use the same search budget and report best hyperparameters per pair and validation curves. If budgets differ, run ablations equalizing them to quantify bias.

concerns.title: Potential overfitting / leakage for learnable probes
concerns.description: Reported gains for learnable similarity and analogy may reflect overfitting or vocabulary overlap between train/test splits (especially in analogy, where shared words can cause leakage), yet the manuscript does not fully document leakage controls or external held-out tests.
evidence: §3.4 notes WordRep authors observed low accuracies and that authors improved scores by training NN; Appendix B indicates computationally intensive NN trained with cross-validation.
Footnote: WordRep splitting approach mentioned but details about ensuring disjoint word sets across splits are limited.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Ensure strict test-time leakage controls: create analogy splits where target words are unseen in training (disjoint word sets), evaluate on external analogy collections not used in tuning, and report per-task learning curves with variance to detect overfitting. Provide ablation showing performance with capacity-limited probes.

concerns.title: Vocabulary intersection and preprocessing bias
concerns.description: Lowercasing and intersecting vocabularies across embeddings may disproportionately remove tokens (rare or morphologically informative) from some embeddings (e.g., morphology-focused or NMT embeddings), altering apparent accessibility and violating injectivity assumptions.
evidence: §3.2 footnote: "Vocabularies were lowercased and intersected before performing experiments. Vectors were normalized to a unit length."
SHARED_ANALYSIS flagged that intersection may bias comparisons.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report statistics: size of intersected vocabulary per embedding, number/type of excluded tokens, and run ablations comparing intersected vs per-embedding vocabularies or controlled subsets (common frequent-only vocabulary) to quantify bias.

concerns.title: Sensitivity of AUC and split-grid choices
concerns.description: Using AUC as the default ordering metric and the chosen training-size grid (e.g., reporting 30%/100% ranks) shapes conclusions about data efficiency; sensitivity to these design choices is not reported.
evidence: §2 suggests AUC as sensible default but paper provides limited sensitivity analysis across alternative aggregations or split points.
PRIOR_STAGE_DIGEST suggested re-running with other split points (10%, 50%) and alternate aggregation metrics.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Show robustness: compute alternate summaries (area under early-range only, win-rate across points, median rank), vary split grid (finer/coarser, include very-small regimes like 1–10%) and report whether ordering conclusions persist.

concerns.title: Generality to contextual/modern embeddings and other languages
concerns.description: Experiments only cover static pretrained embeddings (GloVe, HPCA, NMT, etc.) in English; the proposal's applicability to contextual embeddings (BERT, RoBERTa), fine-tuned representations, or other languages is not demonstrated.
evidence: §3.2 lists static shallow and deep pretrained vectors; contextual embeddings are not included.
Paper's claims are framed broadly about embeddings but tests are narrower.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either temper claims about general applicability or add experiments (or discussion) about how to adapt the protocol to contextual embeddings and multilingual settings (e.g., average/subword pooling probes, freezing vs fine-tuning).

comparable_works.relevance: Supports critique of intrinsic evaluations and motivates need for better probing that correlates with downstream performance.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Chiu et al. show intrinsic metrics fail to predict extrinsic performance—aligns with manuscript's push for supervised, transfer-aligned probes; manuscript extends this by emphasizing sample-efficiency and learnable intrinsic tasks.

comparable_works.relevance: Discusses problems with word-similarity evaluation; manuscript references this as motivation to introduce supervised variants.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Faruqui et al. critique unsupervised similarity datasets; current paper proposes supervised versions that can recover more signal—complementary.

comparable_works.relevance: Provides prior claims that NMT embeddings encode similarity well; manuscript challenges this by showing supervised SVR on GloVe can surpass NMT on SimLex after training.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Manuscript provides a refined perspective: supervised probes can change comparative rankings reported by Hill et al.
comparable_works.source_trace: MANUSCRIPT §3.4 and references to Hill et al.

comparable_works.relevance: Prior conflicting findings about neural vs count-based embedding rankings in different evaluation regimes; manuscript's finding that rankings depend on data size / model class resonates with these mixed reports.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Manuscript offers an explanation mechanism (data-efficiency/model-class dependence) for prior contradictory results.

uncertainty_flags: Generality: limited embedding/task/language coverage; claims about universal applicability are conditional.
Statistical validity: ANOVA-based ranking procedure may violate assumptions and lacks multiple-comparison control details.
Tuning fairness: hyperparameter search budgets per embedding-model pair not reported; possible tuning bias.
Vocabulary preprocessing: lowercasing and vocabulary intersection may unevenly bias embeddings.
Learnable-probe overfitting: gains may reflect capacity/leakage rather than extractable encoded information.
alternative_interpretations: Apparent nonlinear advantages may stem from higher capacity of nonlinear models and better ability to memorize dataset idiosyncrasies (overfitting) rather than intrinsic nonlinear encoding of relations in embeddings.

Rank changes across dataset sizes might reflect differential sensitivity to which tokens are present at different sample sizes (class imbalance, lexicon coverage) rather than fundamental differences in embedding extractability.
Improvements by learnable analogy/similarity could arise from training on overlapping vocabulary/contexts that leak test items rather than from genuinely more extractable relational encoding.
transparency_notes: Authors claim code/results will be released; reviewer cannot verify replication until code and full data splits/hyperparameters are published.
Important operational details (hyperparameter search spaces, per-pair budgets, seeds, exact split-grid) are not fully documented in main text or appendices.
Appendix provides useful NN initialization and formulation for analogy regressor but lacks training curves, early-stopping criteria, and explicit capacity control settings.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The proposal repurposes existing evaluation ideas (probes, learning curves) but their explicit combination (learnable intrinsic tasks + systematic learning-curve AUCs + model-class diversity) is a novel and useful methodological contribution; however novelty does not replace the need for rigorous experimental controls to validate claims.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If ANOVA/ranking artifacts are addressed (robust statistical testing and multiple-comparison correction) and hyperparameter tuning is equalized across embeddings, then observed rank shifts and nonlinear benefits will reflect true embedding properties.
If learnable-probe gains persist under strict leakage controls and capacity-limited probes, supervised intrinsic tasks will reliably reveal additional embedding-encoded information.
If experiments are replicated on contextual embeddings and multilingual datasets showing similar patterns, the protocol could generalize broadly and influence standard evaluation practice.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Combines known evaluation elements in a practical, coherent protocol (learning-curves + supervised probes + model diversity), and demonstrates empirical benefits; this is a pragmatic advance rather than a radical theoretical breakthrough.
evidence: Proposal (§2) integrates prior suggestions (probes, intrinsic critique) and formalizes the objective (Eq.1).
Empirical examples where supervised probes change rankings provide proof-of-concept.
uncertainty_flags: Requires stronger statistical rigor and broader replication (contextual embeddings, other languages) to fully claim general methodological impact.

novelty_lenses.rationale: If validated and adopted, shifting evaluation to data-efficiency and supervised learnable probes could meaningfully change how embedding methods are compared and selected for applications—potentially disruptive—but this impact depends on resolving methodological concerns and demonstrating broad applicability.
evidence: Theoretical anchor (injectivity / Bayes risk) provides conceptual justification.
Empirical results show cases where conventional rankings and conclusions would change.
uncertainty_flags: Current experiments are limited; adoption would require robust, reproducible evidence including modern contextual embeddings.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence reflects that the core idea (evaluating embeddings by data-efficiency and supervised probes) is well-motivated and supported by presented experiments, but important methodological gaps (statistical testing, tuning fairness, leakage controls, and generalization to contextual/multilingual settings) reduce my confidence in the breadth and permanence of the empirical claims until those are addressed.

consensus_findings: The paper is coherent and well-motivated: reframing embedding evaluation around transfer-oriented data-efficiency (learning curves across training sizes) and simple supervised probes is a defensible and actionable proposal.

Theoretical observation (Appendix A) that injective embeddings preserve Bayes risk is correct as presented and provides useful conceptual motivation to focus on learnability/sample-complexity in practice.

Supervised/learnable variants of intrinsic tasks (similarity, analogy) can produce higher measured scores than constant/cosine heuristics in the reported experiments and therefore can reveal information that unsupervised intrinsic metrics miss.

Empirical results show that embedding rankings can change with dataset size and choice of model class (linear vs nonlinear), and that single-word properties are typically learned faster (high early accuracy) than relation-focused tasks such as analogy.

Including multiple model classes (constant, linear, nonlinear) is informative: some embeddings appear to yield gains only with nonlinear probes, implying model-class diversity is a valuable part of an evaluation protocol.
disagreements: Extent and generality of the empirical claims: reviewers differ on how broadly the reported phenomena (e.g., ~11% analogy gains, prevalence of nonlinear encodings, magnitude of rank shifts) generalize beyond the tested set of static embeddings, datasets, languages, and split choices.

Severity of methodological issues: all reviewers flag statistical/preprocessing/tuning concerns, but they disagree on whether these flaws are fatal to the central message (some view them as fixable caveats; others see them as major threats that may materially change conclusions).

Novelty characterization: some reviewers treat the work as a meaningful methodological innovation (combining learning curves + supervised intrinsic probes + model diversity), while others view it as an incremental operational refinement of existing critique-of-intrinsic-eval literature.

Practical interpretability of supervised probes: reviewers disagree on whether supervised, possibly nonlinear probes remain 'simple and interpretable'—some view them as still useful probes; others note that high-capacity probes reduce interpretability and risk conflating probe capacity with embedding content.
uncertainty_hotspots: Statistical aggregation and ranking: the pairwise ANOVA-based greedy grouping and rank aggregation (6 repeats at each split) lack documented diagnostics (normality, homoscedasticity) and multiple-comparison correction; sensitivity to alternative nonparametric or permutation-based tests is untested.

Hyperparameter search parity and tuning budgets: per-embedding/model hyperparameter grids, search budgets, and whether tuning effort is equalized are not fully specified; unequal tuning could bias which embeddings appear to benefit from nonlinear models or small-data regimes.

Vocabulary preprocessing effects: lowercasing, unit-normalization, and vocabulary intersection across embeddings may disproportionately remove or alter tokens (particularly morphological/case-sensitive ones), potentially introducing bias and violating injectivity in practice.

Overfitting/leakage risk for learnable probes: improvements from SVR or neural analogy regressors may reflect memorization, dataset artifacts, or vocabulary overlap between train/test (especially for analogy), rather than recoverable embedding information; held-out/held-vocabulary validation is not fully documented.

Aggregation choice sensitivity: choice of AUC as the default summary metric and the particular split points (e.g., reporting 30% and 100%) could alter rankings; alternative summaries (early-data AUC, win-rate, slopes) have not been exhaustively analyzed.

Generality to modern/contextual embeddings and other languages: experiments focus on static English embeddings; applicability to contextualized vectors (BERT, etc.), multilingual settings, and to embeddings fine-tuned on downstream tasks is uncertain.
model_diversity_effects: Including constant, linear, and nonlinear probe models exposed differences that single-model evaluations would miss: some embeddings show substantial gains only when nonlinear models are allowed, indicating the presence of relation encodings that are not linearly accessible.

However, model-class comparisons introduce role-specific effects: nonlinear probes often have greater capacity and thus a higher risk of overfitting, especially in low-data regimes; distinguishing 'information encoded nonlinearly' from 'nonlinear probe memorization' requires capacity-controlled ablations and held-out validation.

The choice of probe family interacts with hyperparameter tuning: embeddings that appear to benefit from nonlinear probes may partly benefit from more extensive tuning or different default regularization, making parity in tuning critical when interpreting model-diversity effects.

Role-specific implication for evaluation design: evaluating multiple probe classes is informative, but conclusions about embeddings must explicitly account for probe capacity, regularization, and fairness of optimization effort to avoid conflating probe skill with embedding content.
meta_review.editor_guidance: The editor should treat the manuscript's conceptual contribution (data-efficiency + supervised intrinsic probes + model diversity) as promising but contingent on stronger methodological transparency and robustness checks. Request that authors provide (1) full reproducible artifacts (code, exact split seeds, preprocessed vocabularies), (2) diagnostics and alternative analyses for the ranking procedure (tests of ANOVA assumptions, nonparametric or permutation-based rank aggregation, multiple-comparisons corrections), (3) complete hyperparameter search specifications and evidence of balanced tuning budgets (or re-runs that equalize budgets), (4) vocabulary-overlap and collision statistics (pre/post intersection) and ablations showing sensitivity to preprocessing, (5) explicit leakage controls and held-out evaluations for learnable probes (analogy/similarity) including capacity-limited probe variants and external analogy/similarity test sets, and (6) sensitivity analyses for aggregation metrics (early-AUC, win-rate, slopes) and split grids (including very-small-data points). If authors supply these materials and robustness analyses, the work should be considered a solid methodological contribution worth public release as an evaluation protocol; if not, emphasize that conclusions about empirical magnitudes and generality remain provisional.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen evidence and make results reproducible and interpretable, please provide the following concrete items and analyses: (a) release code, processed datasets, exact random seeds, and preprocessed vocabularies (before and after lowercasing/intersection) so reviewers can reproduce learning curves and ranks; (b) publish the full hyperparameter search spaces, per-embedding/model budgets, selected hyperparameters, and validation curves; (c) run and report alternative rank-aggregation/statistical tests (per-curve-point permutation tests or Wilcoxon/Friedman + appropriate multiple-comparison corrections) and show whether ranks and AUC-orderings are stable under these variants; (d) include ablations that avoid full vocabulary intersection (per-embedding vocab experiments or controlled common/rare subsets) and report collision rates (identical or near-identical vectors after normalization) to test injectivity assumptions; (e) for learnable similarity/analogy probes, enforce strong leakage controls (e.g., disjoint word sets where appropriate), evaluate on held-out analogy/similarity corpora not used in tuning, and provide capacity-controlled comparisons (regularized shallow nets, kernel methods with matched capacity) to distinguish genuine nonlinear encoding from overfitting; (f) report alternative aggregation summaries (early-AUC for low-data regimes, win-rate tables, slopes) and show correlations between these summaries and the chosen AUC to assess sensitivity; (g) if compute permits, present at least pilot results on one or two contextual embedding families or explicitly constrain the manuscript's scope to static embeddings and explain adaptation to contextual models; and (h) include compute/time/resource footprints for the more intensive probes to aid reproducibility.
transparency_report: Authors state code/results will be released but the manuscript currently lacks a persistent URL or artifact bundle containing (i) exact random seeds/split definitions used for the 6 repeats, (ii) full hyperparameter search logs and best-parameter records per embedding-model pair, (iii) pre- and postprocessing vocabularies and token counts per embedding, and (iv) per-run raw scores needed to reproduce ANOVA/ranking decisions.

ANOVA-based ranking: implementation details are sparse—diagnostics (residual distributions, variance homogeneity checks), multiple-comparison corrections, and exact pairwise-testing order are not reported.

Learnable-probe training details: appendix gives architecture hints (e.g., analogy NN initialised as 3COSADD) but missing are full training hyperparameters, epochs, early stopping criteria, regularization, held-out validation splits, and training/validation/training-loss curves.

Vocabulary preprocessing: the paper notes lowercasing and vocabulary intersection but does not provide counts of excluded tokens or per-embedding coverage statistics that would reveal preprocessing bias.
Compute/resource reporting: the paper mentions computational intensity (analogy NN) but lacks concrete compute-time, hardware, and approximate cost figures for reproducing experiments.
epistemic_limits: This synthesis is based only on the textual reviews and shared analysis provided; I have not executed the authors' code or re-run any experiments. The reviewers' assessments rely on the reported experimental design and results as presented; discrepancies between reported methods and released code (if any) cannot be detected here. Quantitative assessments (e.g., how much ranks would change under alternative statistical tests) cannot be estimated without re-running the experiments. Also, the set of reviewers are all analysis agents working from the same manuscript and shared extracts; human experimentalists might surface additional practical issues or domain-specific concerns (e.g., language-specific tokenization effects). Therefore, the conclusions above should be treated as an evidence-weighted but ultimately provisional map of agreement, contention, and uncertainty, pending authors' provision of reproducibility artifacts and robustness checks.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript proposes reframing static word-embedding evaluation to emphasize data-efficiency (learning curves across training sizes, summarized e.g. by AUC), simple supervised probe tasks including learnable variants of intrinsic similarity and analogy, and model-class diversity (constant/linear/nonlinear). A short theoretical observation (Appendix A) shows injective embeddings preserve Bayes risk, motivating a focus on learnability under finite data and restricted hypothesis classes. Empirically the authors run repeated-split learning-curve experiments on a battery of 15 datasets and several pretrained static embeddings, report that supervised (learnable) similarity/analogy can improve over constant baselines (examples: SVR, NN regressor), that embedding rankings shift with dataset size and probe model class, and that single-word properties are typically data-efficient while relation tasks (analogy) are much harder. Overall the proposal is a coherent, actionable methodological contribution, but several methodological and reporting gaps temper confidence in the generality and numerical magnitudes of the empirical claims.
strengths: Conceptual reframing aligning embedding evaluation with transfer-usefulness (sample efficiency) and a concise formalization (Eq.1) tying evaluation to classifier families and dataset size.

Clear, implementable protocol: supervised probe variants of intrinsic tasks, explicit model-class diversity, repeated-split learning curves, and an AUC-style summary—facilitates adoption and reproducibility if artifacts are released.

Empirical proof-of-concept showing supervised intrinsic probes can outperform constant heuristics (reported improvements on some analogy/similarity subsets) and that probe model class materially affects measured embedding utility.
Theoretical anchor (Appendix A) correctly states that injective embeddings preserve Bayes risk, usefully shifting focus to learnability and sample complexity as practical discriminants.
limitations: Statistical aggregation and ranking under-specified: ranks are assigned via a greedy pairwise ANOVA per curve point but the manuscript does not report diagnostics (ANOVA assumptions: normality, homoscedasticity), nor multiple-comparison corrections or sensitivity to nonparametric/ permutation-based alternatives—this could materially affect reported rank stability and ordering.

Hyperparameter-search and tuning parity unclear: the paper states cross-validation and fallbacks but does not publish per-embedding/model hyperparameter grids, search budgets, or per-pair best settings; unequal tuning effort could bias which embeddings appear more data-efficient or better with nonlinear probes.

Vocabulary preprocessing risks bias: all embeddings were lowercased, unit-normalized, and intersected before evaluation; the manuscript omits per-embedding coverage statistics and collision rates (post-normalization), so preprocessing could unevenly remove morphology- or case-sensitive tokens and violate the injectivity assumptions in practice.

Overfitting/leakage controls for learnable probes not fully documented: reported gains for supervised similarity/analogy (e.g., ~11% on a subset) may reflect memorization or lexical overlap between train/test (especially in analogy tuples). The paper lacks explicit held-out analogy corpora evaluations, disjoint-word-splits, and capacity-controlled ablations to separate genuine embedded signal from probe overcapacity.
open_questions: Please provide diagnostic evidence for the ANOVA-based ranking: were residuals tested for normality and homoscedasticity, and how do rankings change if you use nonparametric or permutation-based tests (e.g., Friedman/Nemenyi, Wilcoxon pairwise with corrections, or bootstrap)?

Document hyperparameter search: what were the exact hyperparameter grids and search budgets per model-embedding pair, and do rankings/data-efficiency curves change if you equalize the tuning budget across embeddings and probe families?

Provide vocabulary/preprocessing statistics: how many tokens per embedding were removed by lowercasing/intersection; what fraction of dataset items lost coverage per task; and how many collisions (identical or near-identical vectors) occur after normalization?

For learnable analogy/similarity probes, what leakage controls were used? Can you report results on held-out analogy/similarity corpora or splits with disjoint word sets, and include capacity-controlled probe comparisons (e.g., strongly regularized shallow nets or kernel methods) to test generalization vs overfitting?

How sensitive are your conclusions to aggregation choices and split grids? Please report rankings under alternative summaries (early-data AUC, performance at very-small data points like 1%/5%, win-rate, slope) and with alternative split schedules (including finer-grained small-data regime).

How do you recommend adapting the proposed protocol to contextualized embeddings (BERT-family) and multilingual settings—do you expect the same phenomena (nonlinear encodings, rank volatility) to hold, and what probe design changes would you advise?
consensus_snapshot: Conceptual proposal (evaluate embeddings by data-efficiency + simple supervised probes + model-class diversity) is well-motivated and operationalizable.
Supervised (learnable) variants of intrinsic tasks can reveal additional embedding-encoded signal that constant/cosine heuristics miss, per the authors' experiments.
Probe model-class diversity matters: nonlinear probes sometimes extract useful information inaccessible to linear probes, but interpretation requires careful control for probe capacity and tuning.

Single-word properties tend to be learned quickly (high early accuracy) while relation-focused tasks (analogy) require more data/capacity—this pattern is consistently observed in the reported experiments.
disagreement_snapshot: Degree of empirical generality: reviewers differ on whether the observed effects (magnitude of supervised gains, prevalence of nonlinear encoding, and rank volatility) generalize beyond the tested static embeddings and English datasets—some view this as plausible innovation signal, others see the evidence as too narrow for broad claims.

Severity of methodological shortfalls: reviewers agree issues exist (ANOVA, tuning, preprocessing, leakage) but disagree on whether these undermine the central conceptual message (some see them as fixable caveats; others consider them threats to the empirical claims' credibility until resolved).

Interpretability of supervised probes: some reviewers accept supervised probes (even nonlinear) as interpretable/simple enough for evaluation; others caution that high-capacity probes undermine interpretability and can conflate probe learning with embedding content.
uncertainty_snapshot: Ranking sensitivity to statistical aggregation and multiple-comparison procedures—uncertainty until alternative ranking tests and corrections are reported.
Extent to which supervised-probe improvements generalize vs reflect overfitting or dataset artifacts—uncertainty until held-out/held-vocabulary evaluations and capacity controls are provided.
Impact of vocabulary preprocessing on results and on the practical injectivity assumption—uncertainty until per-embedding coverage and collision statistics are published.
Generality to contextualized embeddings, multilingual datasets, and fine-tuned representations remains unknown.

§2 Proposal & Eq. (1) (manuscript): formalization of expectation over classifiers and dataset sizes for evaluation.

§3.4 and Appendix B (manuscript): empirical report of supervised analogy regressor (NN initialized as 3COSADD) and reported average ~11% improvement on tested subset; SVR outperforming cosine on SimLex examples.
§3.3 and §3.5 (manuscript): description of repeated-split learning-curve protocol, ANOVA-based greedy rank grouping, and reported rank shifts (30% vs 100% and AUC summaries).

(2015) on analogy baselines (3COSADD/3COSMUL) referenced and NN initialized to 3COSADD; Faruqui et al. (2016) critique of intrinsic evaluations motivating supervised probes (cited in manuscript).
transparency_notes: The manuscript states code and results will be released, but at time of review no persistent artifact bundle/URL was provided. Key reproducibility artifacts currently missing from the paper: (1) exact random seeds/split definitions for the 6 repeats and the train-size grid, (2) full hyperparameter search spaces and per-embedding/model budgets and selected hyperparameters, (3) pre- and post-processing vocabularies and per-embedding coverage statistics (token counts, collisions after normalization), (4) raw per-run scores used for ANOVA/rank aggregation and diagnostics (residuals, assumption tests), and (5) training/validation loss curves and early-stopping/regularization details for the analogy NN and other nonlinear probes. The editors/reviewers recommend releasing these artifacts alongside the paper.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Treat the manuscript as a promising methodological contribution whose conceptual framing is likely to influence embedding-evaluation practice, but require authors to supply additional reproducibility materials and robustness analyses before broader empirical claims are accepted as established. Specifically request: (1) full release of code, exact split seeds, processed vocabularies, and per-run raw scores; (2) diagnostic checks and alternative analyses for the ANOVA/ranking procedure (nonparametric/permutation tests, multiple-comparison corrections) and a sensitivity study of ranking to aggregation choices; (3) full hyperparameter-search logs and evidence of balanced tuning budgets (or re-runs equalizing budgets); (4) vocabulary-intersection ablations and collision/coverage statistics; (5) leakage controls and held-out evaluations for learnable analogy/similarity probes plus capacity-controlled probe ablations; and (6) if authors wish to claim broad applicability, pilot results or discussion about adapting the protocol to contextual embeddings and multilingual data. If these revisions/artefacts are provided, the work can be considered a robust methodological contribution; if not, emphasize that empirical magnitudes and generality remain provisional.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript and make empirical claims more convincing, please provide the following concrete items and analyses: (a) publish the full codebase, exact random seeds, and preprocessed vocabularies (before/after lowercasing/intersection) so curves and ranks can be reproduced; (b) release per-run raw scores and ANOVA diagnostics (residuals, normality/homoscedasticity tests) and re-compute rankings with nonparametric/permutation-based alternatives and multiple-comparison corrections to show robustness; (c) disclose full hyperparameter grids, search budgets, and selected hyperparameters for every embedding-model pair and, if possible, re-run or present ablations equalizing tuning budgets to rule out tuning-induced artifacts; (d) present vocabulary-coverage and collision statistics and ablations that avoid full intersection (per-embedding vocab experiments or controlled frequency subsets) to quantify preprocessing bias; (e) for supervised analogy/similarity probes, ensure and document strict leakage controls (disjoint-word splits where appropriate), evaluate on held-out analogy/similarity corpora not used in tuning, and show capacity-controlled comparisons (e.g., regularized shallow networks, kernel methods) and training/validation curves to detect overfitting; (f) provide sensitivity analyses for aggregation metrics (early-AUC, win-rate, slope) and split-grid choices (including very-small-data points) so readers can understand how conclusions depend on these operational choices; and (g) if claiming applicability beyond static English embeddings, present pilot experiments or a reasoned discussion on adapting probes for contextual embeddings and other languages. Include compute/resource notes for intensive probes to help reproducibility.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: The paper argues for evaluating static word embeddings by data-efficiency (learning curves/AUC), simple supervised probes (including learnable variants of similarity and analogy), and model-class diversity. Theoretical and empirical evidence is provided showing supervised intrinsic probes recover signal missed by constant baselines, that rankings can shift with dataset size and model class, and that single-word properties are data-efficient while analogy is not.

Strengths: Conceptually well-motivated (transfer-usefulness focus), operationalized protocol, empirical proof-of-concept that supervised intrinsic tasks add signal, and a clear theoretical anchor (injectivity => Bayes-risk preservation).

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
